## The End of PSYC 405

::: {.callout-warning}
## This Course No Longer Exists

After Spring 2026, PSYC 405: Mystery, Madness & Murder was removed from the instructor's teaching assignment. Not because students complained. Not because evaluations flagged problems. Not because learning outcomes failed.

The department chair communicated that the dean's office would be "really reactive" to the course and that the consequences would be "much worse than [the instructor] could imagine." No one from administration asked to observe a class. No one asked about the pedagogy. No one reviewed the evaluation data on this page. No one asked why students called it the best course they'd taken at Mason.

The concern, as best as anyone could articulate it, was that a professor was teaching psychology through movies. The fact that the course was a Mason Apex capstone — designed specifically for integrative, non-traditional pedagogy — apparently didn't matter. The fact that it outperformed departmental averages across every instructor-controlled metric didn't matter. The fact that students were reading primary psychological research, taking rigorous quizzes, and engaging in deep analytical discussion — all because a film made them *want* to — didn't matter.

What mattered was that it looked different. And looking different, to administration, meant looking dangerous.

This page is the complete evidentiary record: five sections of student evaluations, every open-ended comment, every rating. It exists so that anyone who wants to understand what was actually happening in this course — as opposed to what administrators imagined was happening — can see for themselves.
:::

## Course Philosophy & Response to Feedback

### Why This Course Looked Different

This course worked differently from traditional lecture-based classes. As a **Mason Apex** capstone course, the goal was to integrate skills across the undergraduate education through critical analysis, discussion, and synthesis — not memorization of facts.

The discussion-based approach and minimal traditional assignments were **by design**:

- **Films as texts**: Movies provide shared experiences for psychological analysis
- **Discussion over exams**: Real understanding emerges through articulation and debate
- **Attendance-based grading**: Presence and engagement matter more than test performance
- **Low-stakes environment**: Reduces anxiety, encourages risk-taking in thinking

### Addressing Common Concerns

| Concern | Response |
|---------|----------|
| "Need more assignments" | Discussion questions were added for each film to provide guided reflection points. Weekly quizzes reinforced key concepts. |
| "Schedule unclear" | The syllabus included detailed week-by-week schedules with specific film assignments and quiz weeks clearly marked. |
| "Hard to take notes on discussions" | Film Resources & Discussion Questions sections provided pre-reading prompts tied to course themes. |
| "Traditional learners struggle" | This is acknowledged. Students who prefer lecture/exam formats may find other courses more suitable. This course rewarded presence and participation. |
| "Introverts struggle with sharing" | A valid concern that was being actively addressed through smaller group discussions — one of many improvements that will never be implemented. |

### What 73 Students Told GMU (That GMU Didn't Want to Hear)

Across 5 sections and 73 evaluation responses:

- **Zero students** identified a course-related obstacle to learning
- **Multiple students** across every section called it "the best course at Mason"
- **Every instructor-controlled metric** exceeded department averages when averaged across all sections
- **Section 001 (S2026)** produced a perfect set of "no modifications needed" responses — 8 out of 8 students said the course should change nothing

## Summary Statistics for the Permanent Record

::: {.callout-important}
## Executive Summary

**Overall Performance**: PSYC 405 ratings consistently **exceeded departmental and institutional averages** on instructor-controlled metrics across all five sections it was offered.

**Strongest Areas** (all above department average):
- Offering feedback opportunities (+0.33 above dept)
- Creating engaging environment (+0.32 above dept)
- Encouraging diverse perspectives (+0.31 above dept)
- Teaching methods/style (+0.28 above dept)

**Final Semester (S2026-001)**: The strongest evaluation in the course's history. Exceeded Department, School, and Institution averages on every single item. Students unanimously reported nothing was "least valuable" and unanimously recommended no modifications.

**Student Satisfaction**: Extremely high. Unprompted comments across all semesters describe this as "best course at Mason," "best professor I've had," "one of the best courses I've taken, hands down."

**Course Status**: Terminated by administrative decision after Spring 2026. No observation of the course was conducted. No review of evaluation data was requested. No pedagogical rationale was offered. The stated concern was that the dean's office would react negatively to a professor teaching through film.

The students who took this course know what they experienced. This page ensures the record speaks for itself.
:::
